props.title: The Next Best Thing

sections.content: The Next Best Thing (2000) represents a pivotal moment in LGBTQ+ cinema, arriving at the turn of the millennium when mainstream Hollywood was tentatively exploring non-traditional family structures. Madonna and Rupert Everett star in this romantic dramedy that, while flawed, tackled co-parenting and gay parenthood years before The Kids Are All Right (2010) earned widespread acclaim. The film shares DNA with earlier groundbreaking works like Making Love (1982) and Philadelphia (1993), though its lighter tone aimed to make these themes more accessible to mainstream audiences.

sections.content: The film's treatment of alternative family structures echoed through later works like Life as We Know It (2010) and Friends with Kids (2011), though these later films focused more on straight co-parenting arrangements. What makes The Next Best Thing particularly noteworthy is its attempt to blend romantic comedy conventions with weightier themes of custody battles and LGBTQ+ rights, even if the execution sometimes falters.

The casting of Madonna and Rupert Everett capitalized on their real-life friendship and Everett's status as one of Hollywood's few openly gay actors at the time. Their chemistry recalls similar platonic partnerships in films like My Best Friend's Wedding (1997), where Everett memorably played Julia Roberts' gay confidant, a role that helped pave the way for this leading performance. sections.content: Looking at the film's legacy, we can trace how Hollywood's portrayal of LGBTQ+ families evolved from this somewhat cautious approach to more nuanced explorations in films like Beginners (2010) and Any Day Now (2012). While The Next Best Thing sometimes stumbles with dated stereotypes, it helped normalize conversations about non-traditional families in mainstream cinema.
